reportTraitWeight.citation: Weight on the person's traits (speaking out and following the rules against staying quiet) when deciding to report a bribe they refused or were told of. Whistleblowing tracks conscientiousness and moral courage (Bjorkelo, Einarsen and Matthiesen 2010, Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology 83(2):371-394).

spread.citation: The same spread the corruption engine gives its trait weight.

reportTieWeight.citation: Weight on the reporter's closeness to the accused, pulling against reporting: people report strangers far more than friends or kin (Rose-Ackerman and Palifka 2016, Corruption and Government, ch. 9).

spread.citation: The same spread the corruption engine gives its tie weight.

reportDutyPull.citation: The pull to report a bribe one refused as a public official, before traits and ties. About half of the federal public-corruption cases the Justice Department's Public Integrity Section describes began with a report by a participant or a refusing official (Public Integrity Section, Report to Congress 2019, case summaries).

spread.citation: Checked against the share of refused bribes that are reported in a played year.

reportHearsayPull.citation: The pull to report a bribe one was only told of, smaller than for a witness. The Global Corruption Barometer (Transparency International 2019) found most people who knew of corruption did not report it.

spread.citation: Half the witness's pull at the center.

witnessEvidence.citation: Evidence strength, 0 to 1, of a complaint from a party to the act (the official who refused, or a party who took part): direct testimony without documents.

spread.citation: Between hearsay and documents.

hearsayEvidence.citation: Evidence strength, 0 to 1, of a complaint from someone a party told: hearsay alone rarely carries a charge (Federal Rule of Evidence 802).

spread.citation: Half a witness's strength.

paymentEvidence.citation: Evidence strength, 0 to 1, of a payment from the offerer's account to the official's found on the books once an investigation subpoenas them: bank records are the core of most bribery prosecutions (Public Integrity Section, Report to Congress 2019).

spread.citation: Documents short of a recording or confession.

prominenceTown.citation: How much a town or township official's case is worth to a prosecutor, the base the other levels are measured against.

spread.reason: The unit the other prominence levels are measured against; it is fixed at 1 and only the ratios matter.

prominenceCounty.citation: A county official's case against a town official's. Prosecutors weigh a case's public importance (U.S. Justice Manual 9-27.230, the federal interest in a prosecution).

spread.citation: Ordered by the size of the electorate the office answers to.

prominenceState.citation: A state legislator's case against a town official's (U.S. Justice Manual 9-27.230).

spread.citation: Ordered by the size of the electorate the office answers to.

prominenceStatewide.citation: A statewide or federal official's case against a town official's (U.S. Justice Manual 9-27.230).

spread.citation: Ordered by the size of the electorate the office answers to.

prominencePrivate.citation: A private person's case (the one who offered) against a town official's: the official's breach of public trust is the heart of a bribery case (U.S. Justice Manual 9-85.100).

spread.citation: Below any official.

prosecutorPartyWeight.citation: How much less a case is worth to a prosecutor when the accused shares their party: U.S. attorneys investigated and charged officials of the other party more often (Gordon 2009, American Political Science Review 103(4):534-554).

spread.citation: From no bias to Gordon's upper estimate.

prosecutorTraitWeight.citation: Weight on a prosecutor's own traits (confronting against playing safe) when deciding whether a case is worth opening and charging.

spread.citation: Half the reporter's trait weight: the office's standards narrow a prosecutor's own temperament.

investigateBar.citation: The worth an investigation must clear: evidence times the case's prominence, against the office's cost of opening one.

spread.citation: A refused town bribe reported by the official clears it; hearsay about a town official alone does not.

chargeBar.citation: The evidence strength a prosecutor needs to charge: federal prosecutors charge only when the admissible evidence will probably be sufficient to convict (U.S. Justice Manual 9-27.220).

spread.citation: Around more likely than not.

prosecutorLossWeight.citation: How much a prosecutor's share of cases lost at trial raises the evidence they want before charging.

spread.citation: Unmeasured; the direction follows Boylan and Long 2005 on prosecutors' career concerns.

convictionBar.citation: The evidence, net of the defense, a court needs to convict: proof beyond a reasonable doubt, set above the charging bar. About 83% of federal defendants who went to trial in fiscal 2022 were convicted (Bureau of Justice Statistics, Federal Justice Statistics 2022).

spread.citation: Checked against the share of trials ending in conviction.

defenseWeight.citation: How much the defendant's money (against a felony defense's cost) lowers the evidence the court weighs: retained counsel won more acquittals and dismissals than appointed counsel in large urban courts (Bureau of Justice Statistics, Defense Counsel in Criminal Cases, 2000).

spread.citation: Small against the evidence.

defenseCostMinor.citation: What a retained defense through trial in a public-corruption felony costs, $50,000. Felony defense fees run from about $10,000 to well over $100,000 for white-collar trials.
defenseCostMinor.estimatedFrom: Published private defense fee ranges; spread $10,000 to $150,000

spread.citation: From a short felony case to a white-collar trial.

pleaTraitWeight.citation: Weight on the defendant's traits (conceding against confronting) when weighing a plea against trial.

spread.citation: Smaller than the case's own strength: about 90% of federal convictions came by plea (Bureau of Justice Statistics, Federal Justice Statistics 2022).

pleaDiscount.citation: How much shorter a plea's sentence is than the one after a trial loss: federal sentences after trial averaged about three times those after a plea for the same offense (National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, The Trial Penalty, 2018), most of it from charge bargaining; a third off the term is the guideline's acceptance-of-responsibility reduction at its larger end (U.S. Sentencing Guidelines 3E1.1).

spread.citation: From the guideline reduction alone to a typical charge bargain.

severityScaleMinor.citation: The bribe, $10,000, at which its size reaches half its weight in a sentence's severity: the federal fraud and bribery guideline adds offense levels by the value of the bribe, starting above $6,500 (U.S. Sentencing Guidelines 2C1.1(b)(2), 2B1.1(b)(1)).

spread.citation: The first and third rows of the guideline's loss table.

severitySizeWeight.citation: The share of a sentence's severity from the bribe's size; the rest is the office's prominence (U.S. Sentencing Guidelines 2C1.1(b)(2) and (b)(3), the elected-official enhancement).

spread.citation: Size carries more levels than the office in the guideline.

custodyFloorMonths.citation: The longest guideline range at which a sentence of probation alone is authorized, zero to six months (U.S. Sentencing Guidelines 5B1.1(a)(1), Zone A).

probationMinMonths.citation: The shortest probation for a felony, one year (18 U.S.C. 3561(c)(1)).

probationMaxMonths.citation: The longest probation for a felony, five years (18 U.S.C. 3561(c)(1)).

fineMultiple.citation: The fine for bribery of a public official, up to three times the value of the bribe (18 U.S.C. 201(b)); the court sets it by the case's severity.

daysPerMonth.citation: The mean Gregorian month, 365.25 days over 12.

prosecutorCaseloadCapacity.citation: How many open public-corruption matters (investigations and pending charged cases) one prosecutor's office carries before its workload fully weighs against opening or charging another. A small office's handful of white-collar matters at once; the weight below slides, nothing flips at the number.
prosecutorCaseloadCapacity.estimatedFrom: A small-office public-integrity docket; spread 3 to 20 matters

spread.citation: From one prosecutor with other work to a dedicated public-integrity unit.

prosecutorWorkloadWeight.citation: How much a full docket lowers the worth of opening an investigation or charging a target (the load as a share of capacity times this weight). Smaller than the evidence, so a strong case on a busy desk is still pursued.

spread.citation: Unmeasured; the direction follows prosecutors choosing cases under limited capacity.

cooperationSentenceShare.citation: How much shorter the sentence is for a defendant who testifies against another target, on top of the plea discount: the prosecutor's substantial-assistance motion lets a court go below the range (U.S. Sentencing Guidelines 5K1.1); the size of the cut is a game estimate.

spread.citation: From a modest departure to a large one.

cooperationEvidence.citation: How much a cooperating co-defendant's testimony adds to the evidence against the other targets of the same investigation (witness testimony raised hearsay to direct evidence).

spread.citation: Below a recorded payment, above hearsay.

cooperationLoyaltyWeight.citation: How much the closeness to a co-target (from their relationship record) weighs against giving them up for a lighter sentence.

spread.citation: Closeness runs 0 to 1; a close tie should be able to outweigh the cut.

pretrialBailMinor.citation: Median felony bail amount set by state courts in the 75 largest counties, $10,000 (Bureau of Justice Statistics, State Court Processing Statistics 2009, Felony Defendants in Large Urban Counties, Table 14). Stands for the amount a charged official must post to wait out the trial at home.

spread.citation: BJS reports medians from about $5,000 (assault, drug) to $25,000 (murder).
